title: Remember the sabbath
hook: rest as a gift for servants and animals too (Deuteronomy 5:14)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Name, kept holy and not spent. Your line was hallowed. Did a plain yes or no do the work? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

Read the sabbath commandment slowly and look at who's on the list. "Thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, nor thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thine ox, nor thine ass, nor any of thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates." The children. The servants. The stranger at the gate. The donkey. The day off isn't only for the one who owns the house. Then Deuteronomy says why: "that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou." Today: remember the sabbath, and the people who rarely get one.

The sabbath word comes in Exodus 20 and again in Deuteronomy 5, and the two give different reasons. Exodus points back to creation: God made the world and rested on the seventh day, so the people rest too. Deuteronomy points back to slavery: "remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt." Israel knew what endless work with no say was like. So, the reasoning goes, don't do it to anyone else. On that reading, the sabbath isn't only private rest. It's a limit on the boss, including the boss you are. Jesus, criticized when his hungry disciples picked grain on the sabbath, answered: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Rest is a gift, not a trap. Christians keep this commandment in different ways. Churches that gather on Sunday, the day of the resurrection, may call it the Lord's Day and treat it as their day of rest and worship. Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday, the seventh day. Some Christians stop all paid work on their day; others mark it mainly with worship, family and a slower pace. And the commandment was first given to Israel: in Jewish practice, Shabbat runs from Friday evening to Saturday evening. Across all of them, Deuteronomy asks the same question: who gets to rest because of you, and who doesn't?
screen: `MADE FOR MAN, NOT MAN FOR IT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give someone else a rest. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the people whose work makes your week possible: the one who cooks, drives, cleans, answers your messages, cares for your kids or your parents. Who on that list rarely gets a real break? Let one face come clear. Then think of one thing you could take off their plate this week, or one message you could hold until their workday is over. If you pray, you can name them before God. The bell holds the time.
Remember the sabbath. A day of rest, given not only to you but to everyone who works for you, the stranger, and even the animals.
Your line: rest for everyone. Today, do the one thing you thought of: take the task, hold the message, or say plainly, take the evening off. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-seven.

howItsDone: Christians who worship on Sunday keep it as the Lord's Day for worship and rest, while Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keep Saturday; practice ranges from stopping all paid work to a day shaped mainly by worship and family.

notes: Deuteronomy 5:14–15 and Mark 2:27 quoted from the KJV; the hook capitalizes 'Thou' at the start of the quotation. Confirm.
Christian practice: Sunday as the Lord's Day (no 'most' claim), Seventh-day Adventists and Seventh Day Baptists keeping Saturday; confirm names and phrasing. howItsDone avoids a 'most/many' claim.
Shabbat described as Friday evening to Saturday evening; confirm respectful phrasing ('the commandment was first given to Israel').
Original: שַׁבָּת; the note avoids etymology.

Editor pass: 'the commandment appears twice' was too broad (the sabbath command recurs elsewhere in the Torah); now names Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5. 'Often call it the Lord's Day' softened to 'may'; 'Jewish neighbors keep Shabbat' became 'in Jewish practice, Shabbat runs'. Mark does not say the disciples were hungry; Matthew 12:1 does, so it is now cited for the teach and fork.

Audit pass (2026-10-02): hook glossed 'thy stranger that is within thy gates' as 'the visitor'; the Hebrew ger is a resident outsider, not a guest, so it now says 'the stranger at the gate'. Deuteronomy 5:14-15 and Mark 2:27 KJV checked.
